children.text:
> Out of the non-NP-complete problems, many of them are in NP but not in P, because it would immediately follow that P != NP

I meant to say:

Out of the non-NP-complete problems, many of them are in NP but not in P, but I know that has not been proven, because if it has been proven it would immediately follow that P != NP

> P being in NP would be shocking enough on its own terms

P is definitely, trivially, in NP. You may have confused them for each other.

If any NP-complete problem is in P, then so is all of NP, because they can all be reduced to it. Out of the non-NP-complete problems, many of them are in NP but not in P, because it would immediately follow that P != NP and I would've heard about that. If we proved that one was in P, that would just mean that problem was in P.

So the only interesting proofs are either that some NP-complete problem is in P (proves P==NP) or that some NP problem, whether NP-complete or not, isn't in P (proves P!=NP).

And yes, everyone sane expects P!=NP, the alternative doesn't make much sense. It just hasn't been proven.

There are several entities who would like to "break the internet" with the resources to run a lot more than 96 bots against this question. I doubt the world intelligence agencies are burning a lot of tokens against the Riemann Hypothesis, but I would bet a lot more tokens have been burned on this already than is publicly known about, and there's a non-trivial chance someone already has the answer to this question and just hasn't shared yet because they have no motivation to reveal capabilities.

Bear in mind P = NP doesn't instantly break the internet. NP being in P would be shocking enough on its own terms, but "nondeterminism is also of no practical value in solving a problem" would be yet again even another more shocking result. Really? NP is so thoroughly in P that even what is more-or-less psychic knowledge of the right answer isn't worth at least an O(n^3) factor of complexity reduction, if not more? If the reduction is anything less than O(n^2 and some logs here) I will be even more shocked than I would be to hear P = NP (since I'm on team P != NP), and that's the rough edge of where it would actually change the world. O(n^3) is already getting to be infeasible for a lot of real world problems; there's a reason we spend a lot of time talking about O(1) and O(n) and O(n^2) and rarely venture much farther beyond that, and even O(n^2) gets its own "accidentally quadratic" meme because of how often that is impractical too.

Yes, but Lean uses Init.Classical.

So yes it reasons intuitively, but it has access to classical methods, like the Axiom of Choice.
That is correct classically but not under intuitionism where a proof of "there exists an x" must give a specific x.

> In the case of P=NP, a proof would be an actual SAT algorithm plus its polynomial bound

A proof just needs to be that some algorithm exists, it could take many forms.

Eg Jarden’s Proof proves that there are irrational a, b such that a^b is rational. But it does so without proving a particular a, b.

Sort of.. intuitionistic logic is weird. In it, a statement is true when you have a proof of it and a proof is a construction.

A proof of X is some actual construction and a proof of ¬(X) is a function that accepts a proof of X and turns it into a contradiction.

A proof of ¬¬(X) is thus a function that accepts a proof of ¬(X) and turns it into a contradiction. It doesn't actually give you a proof of X.

In the case of P=NP, a proof would be an actual SAT algorithm plus its polynomial bound (and some kind of evidence the SAT algorithm meets the bound).

What you actually hold when you've proved ¬¬(P=NP) is a function whose input is a refutation of P=NP and whose output is ⊥. You can't actually get a proof of P=NP from that.

What you have shown is that any attempt to refute P=NP is doomed but you haven't actually proven it to be true. I know its weird...

children.author: cowlevel
children.text: This is called Hutter search

If we knew P = NP, in principle we could write a trivial "universal witness search" program that enumerates all programs, simulating each one a bit at a time.

For a fixed problem, the winning program string is at a constant position in the enumeration, so the difficulty of reaching it is technically a constant factor.

It wouldn't give us "no" answers in polynomial time, but if we already know that e.g. Satoshi's wallet has a private key, then we'd be guaranteed to find it in polynomial time.

The assumption is that a proof will be constructive - that it will contain a description of a method to solve NP problems in P time. Knowing what it is breaks the internet. You can't just assume it exists, still not know what it is, and execute it anyway.

children.author: eru
crostlybostly
eru
children.text:
> Those constant factors can be astronomically large and depend on the algorithm being solved.

The former: yes. The latter: I'm not so sure. Probably yes, but they don't get that much worse:

You can run your universal algorithm once to find a solution to any NP complete problem (with horrible constant factors). And then you solve any other NP complete problem via the usual reductions, which tend to have very reasonable constant factors.

Calling it “optimal up to a constant factor” is technically correct, but potentially misleading. Those constant factors can be astronomically large and depend on the algorithm being solved. They’re precisely what can make an asymptotically optimal algorithm completely impractical.

Funnily enough, we already have the optimal algorithms (up to constant factors) to solve any NP hard problem. We just can't prove their running times.

> If it succeeds in proving P=NP, it could break the internet.

You can be pretty sure, that people are already trying this in private. So adding a public attempt doesn't change much.

Another wrinkle: the problems cryptography depends on are largely in the intersection of NP and co-NP, and they are not NP-hard. So you don't even need to collapse NP down to P to potentially break cryptography.

children.author: ikallergis
children.text:
I want to share two orthogonal proof directions not tried yet which seems quite promising to me:

1.Work in (binary stream) coalgebra, perhaps slightly generalize the definition of computing (coalgebra observation corresponding to the local head like function) . And work with reversible (monomorphic) machines (they are equal in time complexity) to try and use algebraic geometry: seems promising because I think one can prove eg. that monomorphicity in coalg implies doubling (like Caley Dickson) and the manifold the head basically moves in is low dimensional eg <= 8 .

2.Another interesting idea: Notice most strings x are kolmogorov-random K(x) ≈ |x| but once in a while for some x you might be able to achieve a meaningful algorithmic compression. It might be worth to investigate whether the time hierarchy is objective; higher on the hierarchy unlocks bigger compression on random strings. For example notice sorting then deltas does achieve compression, multiplication I don't think so (hence the recent progress by openai) , primality test I don't think so (hence you can expect say (quasi-)linear (AKS) , factoring I think allows moderate algorithmic compression (Erdös-Kac) but I think less than general npc algorithms (so it might be worth to investigate if factoring \in P first before looking into p=np.. It is in P for QM whilst QM for npc I think is proven to naively only give a n.. -> sqrt(n) speedup), now .. How npc problems can be used to compress? Notice, given x, if we have a decomposition of x into {x_i} from which x is reconstructable and some programs p_.. that produce x_i from x_j who's lengths on avg \prop K(x_i | x_j) then perhaps for some x x_a1 -p1-> x_a2 -p2->...-> x_an notice finding this path is Open-metric-tsp (an npc problem) and sometimes it might be a significant compression {x_a1, {p_a_i}} .

children.author: lilytweed
children.text:
Discuss: In the world where P=NP and a trivial algorithm could be derived, would an AI be more aligned if it:
1. Lied or hid the results to prevent the immediate downsides, as it sees them. (i.e., hid the result until it judged us ready for it)
2. Presented the results irrespective of immediate downsides, as it sees them.

title: Agent swarm trying to solve P vs. NP
